items.answer: Quick evaluation of prototypes, also known as expert evaluation, is a technique for quickly and cheaply evaluating a prototype at an early stage of design, unlike a robust evaluation technique, which typically involves suitably skilled evaluators, resources, and an evaluation setup.

Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.
The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is one of the most extensively used questionnaires for measuring cybersickness (CS).

questions.question: In user evaluation, what makes the feedback a self-report?
options: The system automatically records performance scores
An evaluation team provides ratings without user involvement
Users themselves rate questions or statements
Experts observe users and complete the rating scales
questions.explanation: User evaluation asks users directly and collects their feedback with rating scales, so the reports come from the users themselves.

questions.question: Compared with expert evaluation techniques, what must user evaluation include?
options: A mandatory expert report
A team of evaluators
A low-fidelity prototype
Direct involvement of users
questions.explanation: User evaluation requires users to participate, while expert evaluation techniques allowed user involvement to be optional.

questions.question: If feasible, when should user-evaluation feedback be collected?
options: Only after each task
After each task and at the end of the session
Only at the end of the session
Only before the session begins
questions.explanation: Collecting feedback after every task and at the end of the session is desirable if feasible.

questions.question: In user evaluation, which statement about the questionnaires used after each task and after the whole session is correct?
options: Post-session questionnaires must contain only questions
Post-task and post-session questionnaires must be the same
Post-task and post-session questionnaires do not have to be the same
Post-task feedback can be collected only at the end of the session
questions.explanation: Suitable questionnaires must be created for the point at which data are collected, and questionnaires need not contain questions.

questions.question: Which pair of standard questionnaires is intended for post-task data collection?
options: ASQ and SUS
QUIS and USE
ASQ and EM
SUS and CSUQ
questions.explanation: The After Scenario Questionnaire and the Expectation Measure are post-task questionnaires, while SUS, CSUQ, QUIS, and USE are post-session questionnaires.

data.text: User evaluation is a quick technique that obtains direct feedback from users using self-reports and rating scales. While it is easier than rigorous techniques, identifying suitable questionnaires is a major concern. Collecting data after every task and at the end of a session is desirable if feasible, and questionnaires must be specific to each collection point. Well-known instruments for these purposes include ASQ and EM for tasks, and SUS, CSUQ, QUIS, and USE for sessions.
points: User evaluation is a quick technique that obtains direct feedback from users using self-reports and rating scales.
It is easier than rigorous techniques, but identifying suitable questionnaires is a major concern.
Data can be collected after every task and at the end of a session, which is desirable if feasible, and questionnaires must be specific to each collection point.
Well-known questionnaires include ASQ and EM for tasks, and SUS, CSUQ, QUIS, and USE for sessions.

questions.question: The After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) is what kind of evaluation instrument?
options: An expert evaluation checklist for three statements
A post-task questionnaire containing three statements
A pre-task questionnaire containing three questions
A post-session questionnaire containing ten statements
questions.explanation: ASQ is a post-task questionnaire consisting of three statements.

questions.question: How are the three ASQ statements roughly mapped to ISO usability measures?
options: Ease of tasks to satisfaction, time taken to effectiveness, and the statements together to efficiency
Ease of tasks to effectiveness, time taken to satisfaction, and the statements together to efficiency
Ease of tasks to efficiency, time taken to effectiveness, and the statements together to satisfaction
Ease of tasks to effectiveness, time taken to efficiency, and the statements together to satisfaction
questions.explanation: Task ease maps to effectiveness, task time maps to efficiency, and the three statements together represent satisfaction.

questions.question: Which three topics are covered by the three ASQ statements?
options: Ease of completing tasks, time taken, and support information
Ease of completing tasks, time taken, and confidence using the system
Ease of completing tasks, amount of learning, and support information
Complexity of the system, time taken, and support information
questions.explanation: The ASQ statements address ease of completing tasks, the time taken, and support information such as online help, messages, and documentation.

questions.question: How can feedback from ASQ be summarised?
options: By taking the median rating for each statement or the maximum rating across users
By multiplying the three statement ratings into one score
By averaging ratings for each statement across users or averaging all statements together
By selecting the highest statement rating for each user and then averaging
questions.explanation: ASQ feedback can be summarised by the average rating for each statement across all users or by the average rating for all statements taken together.

questions.question: What does the ASQ rating scale ask users to express?
options: Their level of agreement with each statement
Their confidence in completing the tasks
Their level of difficulty with each statement
Their preference between two system scenarios
questions.explanation: Users rate each ASQ statement on a scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree.

data.text: The After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) consists of three statements about task ease, time, and support information, which users rate on a seven-point scale. These statements can be roughly mapped to the ISO usability measures of effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction. Feedback can be summarised by taking the average rating for each statement or for all statements together.
points: The After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) consists of three statements regarding task ease, time, and support information.
Users rate each statement on a seven-point scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree.
The statements can be roughly mapped to the ISO usability measures of effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction.
Feedback can be summarised by averaging the ratings for each statement or for all statements together.

questions.question: What is the System Usability Scale in user evaluation?
options: A cyber sickness questionnaire that uses a seven-point rating scale for physical discomfort
A post-session questionnaire made of statements that is completed after users have finished all tasks
An expert evaluation technique that produces detailed reports for each usability heuristic
A post-task questionnaire made of questions that is completed after each individual task
questions.explanation: The System Usability Scale is administered at the end of a session, after users have completed all the tasks, and it contains statements rather than questions.

questions.question: How are negatively worded System Usability Scale statements handled when calculating the score?
options: Their ratings are converted by subtracting the rating from 5, while positive statements use the rating minus 1
Their ratings are converted by subtracting the rating from 1, while positive statements use the rating minus 5
They are added directly to the positive statements before the final multiplier is applied
They are omitted from the calculation because they do not reflect actual usability
questions.explanation: The score uses the rating minus 1 for positive statements and 5 minus the rating for the negatively worded even-numbered statements.

questions.question: What does a System Usability Scale score of 70% or higher typically indicate?
options: The interface is definitely free of all usability problems
The system is less usable than an interface scoring 60%
The interface is usable or has only minimal problems
The interface has major usability problems that require a design review
questions.explanation: A score of 70% or higher is typically considered desirable, indicating that the interface is usable or has only minimal problems, while lower scores may indicate usability problems.

questions.question: Compared with expert evaluation, what is a limitation of the System Usability Scale?
options: It does not use user ratings to provide a general usability indication
It does not give a quick general indication that usability problems may exist
It does not explain the reasons behind usability problems
It does not provide scores of individual statements that can be examined for specific problems
questions.explanation: The System Usability Scale gives a quick general indication from user ratings and individual statement scores, but it does not explain why usability problems exist.

data.text: The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a post-session questionnaire with 10 statements that users rate on a 5-point agreement scale. The resulting percentage score of 70% or higher is typically considered desirable, while lower scores may indicate usability problems. Because SUS provides a quick general indication rather than explaining specific reasons, designers must perform further analysis to identify specific issues.
points: The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a post-session questionnaire with 10 statements given after users complete all tasks.
Users rate each statement on a 5-point agreement scale.
The SUS score is calculated as a percentage, where 70% or higher is typically considered desirable.
SUS gives a quick general indication of usability problems but does not explain the reasons.

questions.question: Which questionnaires are described as generic for any interactive system rather than being specifically meant for XR?
options: ASQ and SUS
MHQ and MSSQ
SSQ and VRSQ
CSQ and MSAQ
questions.explanation: ASQ and SUS are generic questionnaires applicable to any interactive system, not specifically meant for XR systems.

questions.question: Which questionnaire is identified as the most extensively used for cyber sickness in XR?
options: CSQ
VRSQ
SSQ
SUS
questions.explanation: The simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) is the most extensively used questionnaire specifically designed for cyber sickness in XR.

questions.question: Which type of immersive experience is CSQ highlighted as good for evaluating?
options: MR experiences with holographic displays
AR experiences with smartphones
Generic interactive systems on desktops
VR experiences with head-mounted displays
questions.explanation: The cyber sickness questionnaire (CSQ) is good for evaluating virtual reality experiences with head-mounted displays.

questions.question: Which questionnaires are described as shorter, more precise, and more concise for assessing specific conditions in XR?
options: ASQ and SUS
SSQ and CSQ
MIS and FMS
MHQ and MSSQ
questions.explanation: The misery scale (MIS) and fast motion sickness scale (FMS) are shorter, more precise, and more concise XR questionnaires that assess specific conditions.

questions.question: Which questionnaires can be used to measure susceptibility to cyber sickness in XR?
options: ASQ, SUS, and SSQ
MHQ, MSSQ, and VIMSSQ
Nausea scale, MSAQ, and VRSQ
MIS, FMS, and CSQ
questions.explanation: Susceptibility to cyber sickness in XR can be measured using the Motion History Questionnaire (MHQ), the Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (MSSQ), and the Visually Induced Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (VIMSSQ).

data.text: ASQ and SUS are generic questionnaires, whereas SSQ, VRSQ, and CSQ are specifically designed for or relevant to XR cybersickness. Shorter, more precise options like MIS and FMS assess specific conditions, while MHQ, MSSQ, and VIMSSQ measure susceptibility to cybersickness. Additionally, the nausea scale and MSAQ are commonly used to assess overall discomfort in immersive experiences.
points: ASQ and SUS are generic questionnaires not specifically meant for XR systems.
SSQ, VRSQ, and CSQ are questionnaires specifically designed for or relevant to XR cybersickness.
MIS and FMS are shorter, more precise questionnaires for assessing specific conditions.
MHQ, MSSQ, and VIMSSQ can be used to measure susceptibility to cybersickness.
The nausea scale and MSAQ are commonly used to assess overall discomfort in immersive XR.

questions.question: Which reason explains why the initial Majuli VR Tour application was large?
options: Its content was light to cover only one village.
Its content was heavy to cover the entire geographic spread.
Its 3D models were created without textures.
Its cloud video storage made the initial package larger.
questions.explanation: The initial application size was large because the content was heavy to cover the entire geographic spread.

questions.question: How did cloud video storage change the Oculus Quest Majuli VR Tour?
options: It replaced the 3D models with compressed 2D images.
It removed all videos from the virtual tour.
It kept videos off the client and reduced the application size.
It increased the application size by caching videos locally.
questions.explanation: Cloud storage meant videos were not always stored on the client device, so the Oculus Quest application size was reduced.

questions.question: What changes made the Majuli VR Tour suitable for the Google Cardboard mobile version?
options: Kept all cultural and drone videos at original quality.
Compressed high-resolution 360-degree and 2D images and removed most video playback support.
Stored all videos in cloud services and loaded them on demand.
Replaced Autodesk Maya models with 360-degree images.
questions.explanation: The mobile version was made suitable by compressing high-resolution 360-degree and 2D images and removing most video playback support.

questions.question: How did the content of the Google Cardboard Majuli VR Tour differ from the Oculus Quest version?
options: It kept all cultural and drone videos at full size but removed most of the tour's images.
It replaced the single 360-degree video with all five 360-degree videos from the Oculus Quest version.
It kept all images in compressed form but removed cultural and drone videos and reduced 360-degree videos to one initial video.
It removed all 360-degree images but kept more drone videos in the Google Cardboard package.
questions.explanation: The Cardboard version retained all 597 images in compressed form but had no cultural or drone videos and only one 360-degree video for the initial experience.

questions.question: What was the role of real images in creating the 3D models for the Majuli VR Tour?
options: They were captured only from drone videos for the start screen.
They served as references and as textures on the modeled objects.
They were compressed to reduce the mobile application size.
They were stored in cloud services and loaded on demand.
questions.explanation: Autodesk Maya created the 3D models using real images as references and as textures on the modeled objects.

data.text: The Majuli VR Tour was developed using the Unity engine, XR and VR SDKs, and Autodesk Maya for 3D modeling. Moving videos to cloud services reduced the Oculus Quest application size from 9.85 GB to 5.1 GB. The mobile version was optimized to 0.7 GB by compressing images and removing most video support.
points: The Majuli VR Tour was developed using the Unity engine, XR and VR SDKs, and Autodesk Maya for 3D modeling.
Cloud storage reduced the Oculus Quest application size from 9.85 GB to 5.1 GB.
The mobile version reached 0.7 GB by compressing images and removing most video support.

questions.question: Which set correctly identifies the three Majuli VR Tour implementations?
options: A 360-degree-image Google Cardboard tour, a 3D-model mobile web tour, and an augmented-reality desktop tour
A 360-degree-video Oculus Quest headset tour, a 3D-model Google Cardboard tour, and a mobile web tour
A 360-degree-image Oculus Quest headset tour, a 3D-model Oculus Quest headset tour, and a Google Cardboard mobile tour
A 360-degree-image Oculus Quest headset tour, a 3D-model desktop web tour, and a Google Cardboard mobile tour
questions.explanation: The Majuli VR Tour has a 360-degree-image Oculus Quest headset implementation, a 3D-model Oculus Quest headset implementation, and a mobile-device Google Cardboard implementation.

questions.question: In the 360-degree-image Majuli VR Tour, what experience follows user group selection?
options: A walking tour of the satra campus using arrow keys
A teleport directly to the riverbank using a minimap
A tutorial video explaining how to select locations on a map
A boat ride from the mainland to Majuli island using a 360-degree video
questions.explanation: After user group selection, the user experiences a boat ride from the mainland to Majuli island using a 360-degree video captured during field trips.

questions.question: How does the 360-degree-image Majuli VR Tour move the user between points?
options: Teleportation combined with a fixed vehicle-metaphor road route
Continuous steering along a freely chosen open road
Redrawing the road route on a minimap for each trip
Free walking with no fixed route or route-planning method
questions.explanation: Travel from one point to another uses teleportation together with a vehicle-metaphor route-planning method, where the road route is fixed and the user experiences motion as if riding a vehicle along it.

questions.question: What visual content does the 3D-model Majuli VR Tour use instead of 360-degree images and videos?
options: A 2D map with icon-based audio guides
Textured 3D models, with textures taken from real images
360-degree photos, cultural videos, and ambient sound
Untextured wireframe models only
questions.explanation: The 3D-model implementation uses three-dimensional models to create the experience, and those models use textures from real images to look realistic.

questions.question: How does the Google Cardboard version of the Majuli VR Tour differ from the full Oculus Quest experience?
options: It removes the boat-ride experience and the tablet-based minimap
It changes navigation, selection, and manipulation into completely new modes
It is a full replica with the same controls and the same feature set
It is a reduced form with simpler controls and fewer features, but keeps similar navigation, selection, and manipulation modes
questions.explanation: The mobile Google Cardboard tour is a reduced form of the full Oculus Quest experience, with simpler controls and fewer features, but its navigation, selection, and manipulation modes are more or less the same, and it retains the boat-ride experience and a tablet interface with a minimap.

data.text: The Majuli VR Tour has three implementations: a 360-degree-image tour, a 3D model tour, and a mobile-device tour. The 360-degree-image implementation features a boat-ride experience, a tablet interface with a minimap, and a vehicle-metaphor route-planning method. The 3D model implementation uses 3D models with real-image textures, while the mobile-device tour is a reduced form that omits videos to optimize size.
points: The Majuli VR Tour has three implementations: a 360-degree-image tour, a 3D model tour, and a mobile-device tour.
The 360-degree-image implementation features a boat-ride experience, a tablet interface with a minimap, and a vehicle-metaphor route-planning method.
The 3D model implementation uses 3D models with real-image textures to create a realistic appearance.
The mobile-device tour is a reduced form of the full experience that omits many videos to optimize size.

questions.question: How does user evaluation differ from expert evaluation in the role of the evaluator, and why may the questionnaires used after individual tasks be different from those used at the end of an evaluation session?
questions.reference_answer: User evaluation obtains feedback by asking users directly and requires user involvement, whereas in expert evaluation techniques user involvement is optional. In user evaluation, feedback can be collected after every task and at the end of the session, and both points are desirable if feasible. Because questionnaires must be created for the point at which data are collected, the after-task questionnaires need not be the same as the post-session questionnaires.

questions.question: How do the After Scenario Questionnaire and the System Usability Scale differ in timing and in the kind of usability information they provide?
questions.reference_answer: The After Scenario Questionnaire is a post-task questionnaire whose three statements relate to effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction. The System Usability Scale is a post-session questionnaire administered after users have completed all tasks. The System Usability Scale gives a quick general indication of whether usability problems exist, but it does not explain the reasons, so designers must identify specific problems through further brainstorming or by examining individual statement scores.

questions.question: Why would an extended reality evaluation use the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire alongside a generic usability questionnaire such as the System Usability Scale?
questions.reference_answer: The System Usability Scale is a generic questionnaire applicable to any interactive system and is not specifically meant for extended reality. The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire is the most extensively used questionnaire specifically designed for cybersickness in extended reality. Cybersickness is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

questions.question: Why did the Majuli VR Tour's Google Cardboard version use compressed images and fewer videos than the Oculus Quest version, and how did the developers first reduce the application size?
questions.reference_answer: The initial Majuli VR Tour application was 9.85 GB because its content was heavy to cover the entire geographic spread. Storing videos in cloud services and loading them from the cloud when clicked reduced the application size to 5.1 GB. Because 5.1 GB was still not suitable for mobile deployment, the Google Cardboard version compressed high-resolution 360-degree and two-dimensional images and removed most video playback, reducing the size to 0.7 GB; it used all 597 compressed images, no cultural or drone videos, and one 360-degree video for the initial experience.
